title: Why the forest monks glow
hookLine: eating once a day, they shine because they don't mourn the past or crave the future (SN 1.10)

lines: ONE MEAL A DAY, IN THE FOREST.
cards: Monks live in the forest. They eat one meal a day, before noon. They sleep on the ground, own a robe and a bowl, and have none of the comforts a person might think they need.

And yet their faces look calm and bright, their complexion clear. You'd expect them to look tired, hungry, worn down. A heavenly being, a deva, can't work it out, so it brings the puzzle to the Buddha.
The answer has nothing to do with food or sleep.

teach.h: WHY IS THEIR COMPLEXION SO SERENE?
teach.b: SN 1.10 is short, a question and two verses. The deva asks: those who live in the forest, peaceful, leading the holy life, eating just one meal a day, why is their complexion so serene? The Buddha answers.

teach.h: NO SORROW FOR THE PAST, NO LONGING AHEAD
teach.b: They don't sorrow over the past. They don't long for the future. They keep themselves going with what is present.
That is why their faces are so clear.
Then a second verse, the other side: those who long for the future and sorrow over the past wither, like a green reed cut down and left in the sun. That picture is precise.
A reed cut from the water still looks green for a while. Then it dries from the inside.

teach.h: THE FACE SHOWS WHAT ISN'T CARRIED
teach.b: Notice what the answer leaves out. It doesn't say the monks are happy because of the forest, or the single meal, or the simple life, though all of that is around them. It points at time.
Two habits wear people down: going back over what's gone, and reaching for what hasn't come. The monks have set down both, and what's left is now, which turns out to be enough to live on.
This isn't a ban on remembering or planning.
Elsewhere the Buddha recalls past lives and makes plans for the community. The verse names sorrowing and longing, the grip, not the memory or the plan. And the glow is a side effect.
Nobody in the story is trying to look radiant. The face just shows what isn't being carried.

how: In the Theravada forest traditions of Thailand and Sri Lanka, many monks still eat a single meal a day and live simply in the forest, and the practice of returning to the present moment is central to their meditation.

games.q: you're a deva puzzled by the forest monks: one meal a day, no comforts, and bright, calm faces. what do you expect the Buddha to say?
o: they don't sorrow over the past or long for the future.
they have special powers from meditation.
games.why: his answer is about time, not food or power: they live on what is present, and their faces show it.

practice: Feel your face, the forehead, the eyes, the jaw, and notice whether any of it is holding something from earlier today, or bracing for something later.
For this one minute, let the past be finished and the future be not yet: when a memory comes, note it, that's past; when a plan comes, note it, that's future; and come back.
What's left is this breath, this seat, this face, softening.

wordCard.voice: Arañña, forest. In SN 1.10, monks there don't sorrow over the past or long for the future; they live on what is present, and it shows in their faces. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali arañña: forest, wilderness. SN 1.10 is called the Arañña Sutta.
